This report compares metaprograms generated from a single cohort across a range of k values.
Here k refers to the number of clusters specified during hierarchical clustering of spectra to define metaprograms. 

Metrics included in this notebook will be used to identify the optimal value of k for this group of samples.

## Set Up

```{r}
# helper function to assign names to a list of file names
assign_k_names <- function(file_list) {
  
  # since nextflow sometimes changes the order of files, grab the value of k from the filename directly here 
  files_n_metaprograms <- basename(file_list) |> 
    stringr::word(1, sep = "_") |> 
    stringr::str_remove("^k-") |>
    as.numeric()
  
  # match name formatting so the ordering is correct in plots
  names(file_list) <- sprintf("k_%02d", files_n_metaprograms) 
  
  return(file_list)
}

# helper function for plotting permutation results
# plots background points with observed values in color on top as sina plot
plot_permutation_results <- function(background_df, pvalue_df, x_axis, y_axis){
  
  ggplot(background_df, aes(x = {{ x_axis }}, y = {{ y_axis }})) +
    ggforce::geom_sina(
      color = "gray",
      alpha = 0.1
    ) +
    geom_point(
      data = pvalue_df,
      aes(
        x = {{ x_axis }},
        y = {{ y_axis }},
        color = is_significant
      ),
      size  = 3,
      shape = 18  # diamond
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "red", `FALSE` = "blue")) +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90)
    )
  
}

# function to calculate the "kneedle"
# copied from https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/ews-nf/blob/main/exploratory-notebooks/05-metaprogram-correlation.Rmd
kneedle <- function(k_values, metric_values, concave = TRUE) {
  
  # Step 1: Smooth data to preserve original shape 
  fit <- smooth.spline(k_values, metric_values)
  metric_values <- predict(fit, k_values)$y
  
  # Step 2: Normalize to [0, 1]
  x <- (k_values - min(k_values)) / (max(k_values) - min(k_values))
  y <- (metric_values - min(metric_values)) / (max(metric_values) - min(metric_values))
  
  # Step 3: Subtract the diagonal (line from first to last point)
  # This "rotates" the curve so the elbow becomes a maximum
  y_diff <- y - x  # for concave (increasing); use x - y for convex (decreasing)
  if (!concave) y_diff <- x - y
  
  # Step 4: The knee is the point with the maximum difference
  knee_index <- which.max(y_diff)
  
  k_values[knee_index]
}


# function to get the max correlation of all cell scores across all mps 
# copied from inside purrr::map in exploratory notebook
# https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/ews-nf/blob/c89ff213b8bf158db0358aa7b4b95577e2e052bd/exploratory-notebooks/05-metaprogram-correlation.Rmd#L193
max_cell_score_correlation <- function(df){
  # turn df into a matrix with cells as rows and metaprograms as columns
  # the contents of the matrix are the cell scores
  mtx <- df |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(
      names_from = "metaprogram",
      values_from = "mp_score"
    ) |> 
    tidyr::unite("cell_id", unique_id, barcodes) |>
    tibble::column_to_rownames("cell_id") |> 
    as.matrix()
  
  # correlation of scores for each metaprogram 
  cor_mtx <- cor(mtx, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  
  # get the non-self max
  diag(cor_mtx) <- 0
  max_cor_df <- data.frame(
    metaprogram = rownames(cor_mtx),
    max_correlation_cells = MatrixGenerics::rowMaxs(cor_mtx)
  )
  
  return(max_cor_df)
}

# helper function to calculate anova on a dataframe
# copied from https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/ews-nf/blob/main/exploratory-notebooks/08-cell-scoring-metrics.Rmd
calculate_anova <- function(df, random_effect = NULL){
  if (!is.null(random_effect)) {
    # create formula with random effect
    formula <- as.formula(glue::glue("log_mean_mp_score ~ disease_timing + (1 | {random_effect})"))
    mod <- lmerTest::lmer(formula, data = df)
    # Overall p-value for disease_timing (type III ANOVA)
    anova_res <- anova(mod) |>
      as.data.frame() |>
      tibble::rownames_to_column("term")
  } else {
    # no random effect so use a regular ANOVA
    mod <- lm(log_mean_mp_score ~ disease_timing, data = df)
    anova_res <- anova(mod) |>
      as.data.frame() |>
      tibble::rownames_to_column("term") |>
      dplyr::filter(term != "Residuals")
  }
  
  return(anova_res)
}

# ANOVA test with/without random effect on log(mean mp score)
# copied from https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/ews-nf/blob/main/exploratory-notebooks/08-cell-scoring-metrics.Rmd
grouped_anova <- function(data, sig_value, random_effect = NULL) {
  
  # for each metaprogram for each value of k, use a linear mixed effect model 
  # then use ANOVA to calculate pvalues 
  anova_results <- data |>
    dplyr::group_by(metaprogram, n_metaprograms) |>
    # using a lambda function requires two arguments
    # can use ... to absorb the second one
    dplyr::group_modify(\(df, ...) {
      calculate_anova(df, random_effect)
    }) |>
    # classify as significant or not
    dplyr::rename(f_value = `F value`, p_value = `Pr(>F)`) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      p_adj = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH"),
      p_adj_signif = dplyr::if_else(p_adj <= sig_value, "*", "ns")
    ) 
  
  full_results <- anova_results |>
    # join with data/scores for plotting 
    dplyr::left_join(
      data |>
        # we'll plot with zscore so want to use that to determine the y position of the label
        dplyr::summarize(
          max_mean_score = max(zscore_mean_mp_score, na.rm = TRUE),
          .by = c("n_metaprograms", "metaprogram")
        )
    )
  
  return(full_results)
}

# calculate significance for permutation testing
# reports a pvalue for a specified statistic 
# copied from https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/ews-nf/blob/main/modules/metaprograms/resources/usr/bin/04-metaprogram-metrics.R
# used here for overall gene set specificity and cell score CV 
calculate_permutation_significance <- function(
  stat, 
  observed_df, 
  background_df, 
  nreps, 
  group_columns = c("n_metaprograms", "metaprogram")
){
  
  # combine the observed values with the background
  combined_df <- observed_df |> 
    dplyr::select(
      dplyr::all_of(group_columns),
      obs_value = {{ stat }}
    ) |> 
    dplyr::left_join(background_df, by = group_columns) |> 
    dplyr::select(-replicate)
  
  # calculate the pvalue for num genesets 
  pvalue_df <- combined_df |> 
    dplyr::mutate(
      # indicate which rows have background > or < obs
      greater_than_obs = {{ stat }} >= obs_value,
      lower_than_obs = {{ stat }} <= obs_value
    ) |> 
    dplyr::summarize(
      # calculate p values and retain a column with the observed value
      obs_value = unique(obs_value),
      greater_pvalue = (sum(greater_than_obs) +1)/(nreps + 1),
      lower_pvalue = (sum(lower_than_obs) + 1)/(nreps + 1),
      overall_pvalue = min(greater_pvalue, lower_pvalue) * 2,
      .by = dplyr::all_of(group_columns)
    ) |> 
    # add adjusted pvalue 
    # depending on the stat will depend on which pvalue we use, either 1 or 2 sided test
    dplyr::mutate(
      greater_adj_pvalue = p.adjust(greater_pvalue, method = "BH"), 
      lower_adj_pvalue = p.adjust(lower_pvalue, method = "BH"),
      overall_adj_pvalue = p.adjust(overall_pvalue, method = "BH")
    )
  
  return(pvalue_df)
  
}
```

## Sample and patient diversity 

Metaprograms should be representative of a diverse set of samples and patients. 
This section will summarize the proportion of samples and patients found in each metaprogram. 
Any metaprograms that are only defined by a single patient will be flagged.

```{r}
# display total samples and patients
# compute this number from the proportion of samples/patients in each metaprogram
total_samples <- metrics_list |> 
  purrr::map_dbl("total_samples") |> 
  unique()

total_patients <- metrics_list |> 
  purrr::map_dbl("total_patients") |> 
  unique()

knitr::asis_output(
  glue::glue("The metaprograms explored here are comprised of **{total_samples} samples** from **{total_patients} patients**.")
)
```


### Proportion of samples 

Here each dot is a metaprogram and the value indicated is the proportion of total **samples** represented by spectra in that metaprogram. 
The dotted line indicates 10% which may help identify any metaprograms with a low representation of samples and/or patients. 

```{r}
ggplot(mp_metrics_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = proportion_of_samples)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm() +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Proportion of total samples \n contributing to each metaprogram"
  )  +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.1, linetype = "dashed")
```

### Proportion of patients 

Here each dot is a metaprogram and the value indicated is the proportion of total **patients** represented by spectra in that metaprogram. 
Again, the dotted line indicates 10%. 

```{r}
ggplot(mp_metrics_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = proportion_of_patients)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm() +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Proportion of total patients \n contributing to each metaprogram"
  )  +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.1, linetype = "dashed")
```

The below table reports how many metaprograms are driven by a single patient and the minimum number of patients represented in a metaprogram for a given value of k. 

```{r}
mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    single_patient_mps = sum(num_patients == 1),
    min_num_patients_per_mp = min(num_patients),
    min_proportion_patients_per_mp = min(num_patients)/total_patients
  ) |> 
  DT::datatable(
    colnames = c("k", "Metaprograms from 1 patient", "Minimum number of patients observed in a metaprogram", "Minimum % of patients observed in a metaprogram")
  ) |> 
  DT::formatPercentage("min_proportion_patients_per_mp")
```

### Normalized effective sample size 

Here we will look at the normalized effective species size or Hill number of order 1. 
This is calculated by taking the exponential of Shannon's entropy and represents the effective number of common or abundant samples. 
Here we are looking for a number close to the total possible samples in that metaprogram. 
The values are normalized by the total number of samples in the metaprogram such that values close to 1 indicate all samples are equally abundant.

To determine if the observed effective sample size is not due to random chance, we performed permutation testing. 
The spectra assigned to each metaprogram were shuffled while preserving the total number of spectra assigned to each metaprogram. 
After shuffling, the normalized effective sample size was calculated to create a null distribution. 

The observed value was compared to the null distribution to get an empirical p-value, producing a single p-value for each metaprogram within a value of k.
The below plot shows both the null distribution in gray and the observed value for each metaprogram. 
The observed values are colored in red if they are significantly greater than the null distribution. 


```{r}
# pull out observations and add in significance column
neff_obs_df <- mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::select(n_metaprograms, metaprogram, eff_number_norm, greater_adj_pvalue_eff_number_norm) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    is_significant = greater_adj_pvalue_eff_number_norm <= sig_value
  )

# get background for all values of k
neff_background_df <- metrics_list |> 
  purrr::map("background_mp_stats_df") |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "n_metaprograms")
```


```{r}
#| fig.height: !r dynamic_fig_height
#| fig.width: 15

plot_permutation_results(neff_background_df, neff_obs_df, metaprogram, eff_number_norm) +
  facet_wrap(vars(n_metaprograms), scale = "free_x", ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    y = "Normalized effective sample size",
    x = "Metaprogram",
    color = "significant"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 14)
  )
```

We then can identify the percentage of metaprograms for each value of k that have a significant normalized effective sample size. 
This will be used to identify the optimal value of k in the final section. 

```{r}
# save to a separate data frame to combine with all metrics at the end
neff_sig_df <- neff_obs_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    neff_sig_number = sum(is_significant), 
    neff_sig_proportion = neff_sig_number/dplyr::n()
  ) 

neff_sig_df |> 
  DT::datatable(colnames = c("k", "Number of metaprograms with significant effective sample size", "% of metaprograms with significant effective sample size")) |> 
  DT::formatPercentage("neff_sig_proportion", 2)
```

## Correlation 

Metaprograms should be unique and non-redundant. 
Therefore we expect them to have low correlation to other metaprograms from the same value of k.

### Gene weights

Here the pairwise correlation of gene weights across all metaprograms was calculated. 
The plot then shows the maximum correlation value for each metaprogram. 
Metaprograms with a max correlation of > 0.5 are considered redundant. 
The number of metaprograms above this cutoff will be used to determine the optimal value of k. 


```{r}
correlation_df <- mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    is_passing = max_correlation <= 0.5
  )

ggplot(correlation_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = max_correlation)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(aes(color = is_passing)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "red", `TRUE` = "black")) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Max correlation of metaprogram gene weights",
    color = "Max correlation ≤ 0.5"
  )
```

```{r}
# save to use with final metrics at the end
grouped_correlation_df <- correlation_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    num_passing_correlation = sum(is_passing),
    proportion_passing_correlation = num_passing_correlation/dplyr::n()
  ) 

grouped_correlation_df |> 
  DT::datatable(colnames = c("k", "Number of metaprograms with max correlation ≤ 0.5", "% of metaprograms with max correlation ≤ 0.5")) |> 
  DT::formatPercentage("proportion_passing_correlation", 2)
```


### Cell scores

The gene weights for the top 200 genes are used to calculate a cell score for each cell in the dataset. 
This is done by taking the dot product of the gene weights and quantile-normalized counts in each cell. 

Here we calculate the pairwise correlation of the scores for all metaprograms to all other metaprograms in the same value of k. 
The plot below shows the max correlation observed for each metaprogram. 
Non-overlapping gene sets may have highly correlated expression.
This statistic will not be used to define the optimal value of k, as we cannot tell from this statistic alone whether the high correlation is due to the two metaprograms sharing the same set of genes or to correlated expression of the two gene sets.

```{r}
# separately calculate the correlation of metaprograms for each value of k 
# then get the max for each metaprogram and combine back into a single df for plotting
score_correlation_df <- scores_df_list |> 
  purrr::map(max_cell_score_correlation) |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "n_metaprograms")

ggplot(score_correlation_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = max_correlation_cells)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm() +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Max correlation of cell scores"
  )
```


## Coherence 

Metaprograms should show coherence, meaning the spectra that comprise the metaprogram are more similar to other spectra in the same metaprogram than to spectra in different metaprograms. 
To measure this, we calculated the correlation of each spectra to all other spectra. 
We then calculate the difference in medians between the distribution of correlation of spectra within a given metaprogram and between metaprograms, indicated as "coherence" throughout this report. 

Metaprograms with coherence <= 0.1 are likely to represent noise and will not be used in further analysis.

```{r}
coherence_df <- mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    is_passing = median_difference > 0.1
  )

ggplot(coherence_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, y = median_difference)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(aes(color = is_passing)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "black")) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Metaprogram coherence",
    color = "Coherence > 0.1"
  ) 

```

This plot suggests that increasing k doesn't improve metaprogram coherence after certain values of k. 
We therefore make an elbow plot showing the median coherence for each value of k and find the elbow.

```{r}
# get the median coherence for each value of k to plot
coherence_elbow_df <- mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    median_coherence = median(median_difference)
  ) |> 
  dplyr::arrange(desc(median_coherence))
```

```{r}
ggplot(coherence_elbow_df, aes(x = n_metaprograms, median_coherence)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Number of metaprograms (k)",
    y = "Median coherence"
  )
```

We then use a modified version of the [kneedle algorithm](https://raghavan.usc.edu/papers/kneedle-simplex11.pdf) to identify the elbow. 
Here we only find one global maximum rather than a set of local maxima. 
Values of k greater than the elbow indicate no substantial gain of coherence over the lower values of k. 

```{r}
# pull out k as numeric
elbow_value <- stringr::str_remove(coherence_elbow_df$n_metaprograms, "k_") |> 
  as.numeric() |>
  kneedle(
    coherence_elbow_df$median_coherence, 
    concave = TRUE
  )

knitr::asis_output(
  glue::glue("**Value of k corresponding to the elbow: {elbow_value}**")
)
```

This plot shows the relationship of coherence with number of patients represented in a metaprogram. 
A negative correlation would suggest that metaprograms specific to a smaller subset of patients tend to have higher coherence, potentially reflecting patient-specific biological signals rather than broadly shared ones.
The R-squared shown in the plot indicates the strength of the correlation. 
The `*` indicates the slope is significantly different from zero, and the `ns` indicates the slope is not significantly different from zero.

```{r}
#| fig.height: 10
#| message: false

# calculate the r2 and pvalue 
patient_coherence_df <- mp_metrics_df |>
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |>
  dplyr::summarize(
    # run lm each time since we can't store the results directly in the data frame
    r_squared = summary(lm(median_difference ~ num_patients))$r.squared,
    p_value = summary(lm(median_difference ~ num_patients))$coefficients["num_patients", "Pr(>|t|)"], 
    # identify any where the slope is significantly different from 0
    sig_label = dplyr::if_else(p_value <= sig_value, "*", "ns"),
    # make a label for the facets
    plot_label = glue::glue("R^2=='{round(r_squared, 3)} {sig_label}'")
  )

# plot the coherence x number of patients
ggplot(mp_metrics_df, aes(x = num_patients, y = median_difference)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(vars(n_metaprograms)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  geom_text(
    data = patient_coherence_df,
    aes(label = plot_label),
    x = -Inf, y = Inf,
    hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1.5,
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    parse = TRUE, # to let us show R2 properly
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of patients",
    y = "Coherence"
  ) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0))
```

## Gene set specificity 

After generating metaprograms for each value of k, the top 200 genes based on gene weights were extracted from each metaprogram. 
Over-representation analysis was then run using `clusterProfiler::enricher()` function on these 200 genes.
Input gene sets include a set of custom `EWS::FLI1` activated and repressed gene sets and Hallmarks from `MSigDb`.

Any gene sets with an adjusted p value ≤ 0.05 are considered significant. 
Good metaprograms should have at least one significant gene set.

The table below shows the total number of metaprograms with at least one significant gene set for each value of k.

```{r}
mp_metrics_df |>
  dplyr::summarize(
    num_metaprograms_with_genesets = sum(num_sig_genesets > 0),
    proportion_metaprograms_with_genesets = num_metaprograms_with_genesets/dplyr::n(),
    .by = c("n_metaprograms")
  ) |> 
  DT::datatable(colnames = c("k", "Number of metaprograms with ≥ 1 significant gene set", "% of metaprograms with ≥ 1 significant gene set")) |>
  DT::formatPercentage("proportion_metaprograms_with_genesets", 2)
```


Metaprograms should be biologically distinct and annotated by a unique set of gene sets.
This means gene sets should be significant in as few metaprograms as possible, ideally only one metaprogram. 
For each gene set, we calculated gene set specificity using the following formula: 

$$1 - \frac{\text{# of metaprograms the gene set is significant in}- 1}{\text{total # of metaprograms} - 1}$$

A score of 1 indicates the gene set is unique to a single metaprogram, while a score of 0 indicates it is shared across all metaprograms. 

We then take the mean specificity across all gene sets and all metaprograms for a single value of k.
Metaprograms with no identified gene sets are not considered in this calculation.

To determine if this value is greater than what would be observed by random chance, we generated a null distribution by shuffling the gene sets assigned to each metaprogram, keeping the number of gene sets consistent with the observed distribution and recalculating the mean specificity. 
When shuffling the gene sets, each gene set was weighted based on the number of metaprograms in which the gene set was considered significant.

The below plot shows the observed mean gene set specificity and the associated background distribution for each value of k. 
Any values of k with a significant mean gene set specificity are indicated in red.

```{r}
# pull out observations and summarize to get the mean for each value of k
gss_obs_df <- mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    overall_geneset_specificity = mean(mean_geneset_specificity, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c("n_metaprograms")
  )

# get background mean gene expression for each k and each replicate
gss_background_df <- metrics_list |> 
  purrr::map("background_specificity_df") |> 
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "n_metaprograms") |> 
  # overall_geneset_specificity is per k
  dplyr::select(n_metaprograms, replicate, overall_geneset_specificity) |> 
  unique()

# pull out the number of replicates 
# note this isn't stored as a number in the objects 
nreps <- max(gss_background_df$replicate |> as.numeric())

# join observed values with background values
# here we are calculating the overall mean pvalue so that we get one pvalue for each k
# this mirrors what we did in: https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/ews-nf/blob/main/exploratory-notebooks/06-gene-set-uniqueness.Rmd
# the metrics calculation script calculates per mp so we need to do this separately here
gss_pvalue_df <- calculate_permutation_significance(
  overall_geneset_specificity, 
  gss_obs_df, 
  gss_background_df, 
  nreps, 
  group_columns = "n_metaprograms"
) |> 
  dplyr::rename(
    overall_geneset_specificity = obs_value
  ) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    is_significant = overall_adj_pvalue <= sig_value
  )
```


```{r}
plot_permutation_results(gss_background_df, gss_pvalue_df, n_metaprograms, overall_geneset_specificity) +
  labs(
    y = "Mean gene set specificity",
    x = "Metaprogram",
    color = "significant"
  ) 
```


## Variation in cell scores 

As noted in the correlation section, the gene weights for the top 200 genes are used to calculate a cell score for each cell in the dataset. 
This is done by taking the dot product of the gene weights and quantile-normalized counts in each cell. 

Good metaprograms should show variation in the scores assigned to cells in the original dataset.
To measure variation, we will use the coefficient of variation (CV), which reports a score's variance relative to the mean score across all cells. 

Here we compare the observed CV to a null distribution to determine if a metaprogram shows significantly more variation compared to random chance. 
The background distribution was constructed by shuffling the gene identifiers for each metaprogram in the gene by metaprogram matrix. 
This ensured that both the weights for each metaprogram and the relationship of genes across metaprograms were retained. 
After shuffling, the top 200 genes were extracted, and the scores were re-calculated. 
This produces a unique background distribution for each metaprogram.

```{r}
# calculate CV for each metaprogram for each sample using Chan's algorithm 
# originally explored in https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/ews-nf/blob/main/exploratory-notebooks/08-cell-scoring-metrics.Rmd
# get both CV and var 
global_background_df <- background_df |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    n_total = sum(num_cells),
    global_mean = sum(num_cells * mean_mp_score) / sum(num_cells),
    M2_total = sum(M2) + sum(num_cells * (mean_mp_score - global_mean)^2),
    score_var = M2_total / (n_total - 1),
    global_sd  = sqrt(score_var),
    score_cv  = (global_sd / global_mean),
    .by = c("n_metaprograms", "metaprogram", "replicate")
  )

# calculate variance and CV for each sample without using Chan's 
# we confirmed previously that this calculation is equal to the result you get from Chan's
# so we can use this as the observed value and then compare to the null distribution
var_df <- scores_df |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    score_var = var(mp_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    score_cv = sqrt(score_var) / mean(mp_score),
    .by = c("n_metaprograms", "metaprogram")
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
```

```{r}
#| fig.height: !r dynamic_fig_height
#| fig.width: 15

# calculate pvalues for each cv 
cv_pvalue_df <- calculate_permutation_significance(score_cv, var_df, global_background_df, nreps) |> 
  dplyr::rename(score_cv = obs_value) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    is_significant = greater_adj_pvalue <= sig_value
  )

plot_permutation_results(global_background_df, cv_pvalue_df, metaprogram, score_cv) +
  facet_wrap(
    vars(n_metaprograms),
    scales = "free_x",
    ncol = 4
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Metaprogram",
    y = "Coefficient of variation (CV)",
    color = "Significant"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 14)
  )
```

The below table shows the total percentage of metaprograms with significant CV for each value of k. 

```{r}
# save to use with final metrics at the end
cv_sig_df <- cv_pvalue_df |> 
  dplyr::group_by(n_metaprograms) |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    num_significant_cv = sum(is_significant),
    proportion_significant_cv = num_significant_cv/dplyr::n()
  ) 

cv_sig_df |> 
  DT::datatable(colnames = c("k", "Number of metaprograms with significant CV", "% of metaprograms with significant CV")) |> 
  DT::formatPercentage("proportion_significant_cv", 2)
```

### Comparison of scores across sample types 

Here we look at the distribution of cell scores across varying sample types (primary, metastatic, and recurrent tumors). 
First, we calculate the mean score for each metaprogram for each sample. 
As the scores are skewed towards zero, we log-transform the scores before calculating any statistics. 
We then compare scores to determine if any metaprograms show significantly different distributions across sample types. 
For the statistical test, we use a linear mixed model with patient as the random effect to account for within-patient correlation that is likely observed in samples of different sample types from the same patient. 

For visualization purposes, we calculate a z-score for all `log(mean(scores))` within each metaprogram and display that in the box plot below.
The significance of the comparison among the three sample types is shown above the distributions for that metaprogram with `*` indicating that the distributions are significantly different from each other and `ns` indicating the distributions are not significantly different from each other. 

**Caution:** This information will not be used to decide on the value of k, but can be helpul to determine if any of the identified metaprograms may be biologically relevant. 
Because we summarize scores for all cells in a sample, this does not tell us anything about the heterogeneity of scores within a sample. 
Further analysis is needed to look at individual cell populations that is outside the scope of the analysis done here.

```{r}
#| eval: FALSE
mean_scores_df <- scores_df |> 
  dplyr::summarize(
    mean_mp_score = mean(mp_score),
    .by = c("unique_id", "metaprogram", "n_metaprograms")
  ) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    scpca_sample_id = stringr::word(unique_id, -1, sep = "-"),
    # first log transform
    log_mean_mp_score = log(mean_mp_score)
  ) |>
  # z-score the log scores within each k and metaprogram
  # use these for plotting
  dplyr::mutate(
    zscore_mean_mp_score = scale(log_mean_mp_score), 
    .by = c("metaprogram", "n_metaprograms")

  # add in the sample metadata including disease timing and patient information 
  dplyr::left_join(
    dplyr::select(
      sample_df, 
      c("scpca_sample_id", "participant_id", "disease_timing")
    ), 
    by = c("scpca_sample_id")
  )
```

## Combining metrics to identify an optimal value of k

In this section, we will combine some of the above metrics to define the optimal value of k. 
Each metric will have a single number reported for each value of k on a 0-1 scale where 1 indicates a good metaprogram. 
The values we will include are: 

* `Effective sample size`: Proportion of metaprograms with a normalized effective sample size significantly greater than the null distribution (p ≤ 0.05).
* `Correlation`: Proportion of metaprograms with a max correlation to all other metaprograms < 0.5.
* `Coherence`: Value indicating if the specific k is at, above, or below the elbow point for coherence. 
The value of k at the elbow is prioritized and assigned a value of 1. 
Values of k below the elbow will be 0.5 and values above the elbow will be 0.
* `Gene set specificity`: Binary value indicating if the overall gene set specificity is significantly greater than the null distribution (p ≤ 0.05).
Values of k that are significant will be 1 and those that are not significant will be 0.
* `Coefficient of variation`: Proportion of metaprograms with a CV significantly greater than the null distribution (p ≤ 0.05).

For each metric, we will rank each value of k, assigning the same rank to any values of k with the exact same value for a specific metric. 
We normalize this value by the total number of possible k so that the scale is still 0-1, where 1 indicates a good metaprogram.
The optimal value of k is the k with the highest average rank.

```{r}
# define the metrics that we are going to use and the order we want to display them 
# make the names human readable for display in the heatmap
metrics_columns <- c(
  "Effective sample size" = "neff_sig_proportion", 
  "Correlation" = "proportion_passing_correlation",
  "Coherence" = "coherence_elbow_passing",
  "Gene set specificity" = "gss_significant",
  "Coefficient of variation" = "proportion_significant_cv"
)

# pull out metaprograms that are significant for gene set specificity
gss_sig_values <- gss_pvalue_df |>
  dplyr::filter(is_significant) |> 
  dplyr::pull(n_metaprograms)

# combine all relevant metrics into a single dataframe
# neff, correlation, and cv sig are already formatted with n_metaprograms and proportion
combined_metrics_df <- neff_sig_df |> 
  dplyr::left_join(grouped_correlation_df, by = c("n_metaprograms")) |> 
  dplyr::left_join(cv_sig_df, by = c("n_metaprograms")) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    # coherence and gss have to be classified by seeing if the value of k 
    # is significant or below/above the elbow 
    k = stringr::str_remove(n_metaprograms, "k_") |> as.numeric(),
    coherence_elbow_passing = dplyr::case_when(
      k == elbow_value ~ 1,
      k < elbow_value ~ 0.5,
      k > elbow_value ~ 0
      ) ,
    gss_significant = as.integer(n_metaprograms %in% gss_sig_values)
  )
```

```{r}
# remove the names for doing the ranks
# having a named list of columns does wierd things with mutate across
rank_metrics_columns <- unname(metrics_columns)
# get the ranks for all metrics columns
# normalize by the max ranks
rank_mtx <- combined_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::select(
    n_metaprograms,
    dplyr::all_of(rank_metrics_columns)
  ) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(
      dplyr::all_of(rank_metrics_columns),
      # normalize so that higher values get higher ranks 
      # ultimately high ranks get a value of 1 and low ranks get a value of 0
      \(column) {rank(column, ties = "max")/dplyr::n()} # exact ties get the same highest rank
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    total_mean_rank = rowMeans(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(rank_metrics_columns)))
  ) |> 
  tibble::column_to_rownames("n_metaprograms") |> 
  as.matrix() |> 
  t()
```



```{r}
#| fig.width: 10

# define a color scale
col_fun <- circlize::colorRamp2(
  breaks = c(0, 0.75, 1),
  colors = c("#2166AC", "white", "#B2182B")
)

# make the heatmap
ht <- ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(
  rank_mtx,
  name = "Value", 
  row_labels = c(names(metrics_columns), "Mean rank"),
  col = col_fun,
  # don't cluster and preserve our ordering
  cluster_rows    = FALSE,
  cluster_columns = FALSE,
  # Split last row into its own section
  row_split = c(rep("Metrics", nrow(rank_mtx) - 1), "Mean rank"),
  row_gap   = unit(0.3, "cm"),  # gap size between the two sections
  # Labels
  row_names_side    = "left",
  column_names_side = "bottom",
  row_names_gp      = grid::gpar(fontsize = 10),
  column_names_gp   = grid::gpar(fontsize = 10),
  column_names_rot  = 90,
  # Cell appearance
  rect_gp = grid::gpar(col = "white", lwd = 2), # white cell border
  border  = FALSE, # no border around the whole thing
  # Legend
  heatmap_legend_param = list(
    title          = "Value",
    title_position = "leftcenter-rot", # rotate title on left
    legend_height  = unit(4, "cm"),
    at             = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1),
    labels         = c("0", "0.25", "0.5", "0.75", "1")
  ),
  # Axis labels
  row_title      = "Metric",
  row_title_side = "left",
  row_title_gp   = grid::gpar(fontsize = 11),
  # Square cells: set a fixed size per cell
  cell_fun = NULL,
  width  = unit(ncol(rank_mtx) * 0.8, "cm"),  # 0.8 cm per column
  height = unit(nrow(rank_mtx) * 0.8, "cm")   # 0.8 cm per row (same as width = square)
)

ComplexHeatmap::draw(ht, heatmap_legend_side = "right")
```

```{r}
# turn the mean back into a dataframe to get the optimal k
# this is the one with max mean score
optimal_k <- rank_mtx |> 
  t() |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  tibble::rownames_to_column("n_metaprograms") |> 
  dplyr::filter(total_mean_rank == max(total_mean_rank)) |> 
  # account for any ties and take the one with the highest rank in proportion significant cv
  dplyr::slice_max(proportion_significant_cv, n = 1) |> 
  dplyr::pull(n_metaprograms)

# find any metaprograms that are patient specific 
single_patient_mps <- mp_metrics_df |> 
  dplyr::filter(num_patients == 1, n_metaprograms == optimal_k) |> 
  dplyr::pull(metaprogram)

# find any metaprograms that have low coherence 
low_coherence_mps <- coherence_df |> 
  dplyr::filter(!is_passing, n_metaprograms == optimal_k) |> 
  dplyr::pull(metaprogram)
```

```{r}
# compile text based on if there are any metaprograms with low coherence or patient specific
main_text <- glue::glue(
  "**The optimal value of k for this cohort is: {optimal_k}**"
)

patient_text <- glue::glue(
  "This value of k has {length(single_patient_mps)} patient-specific metaprograms, which occur when all spectra come from a single patient."
)

if (length(single_patient_mps) > 0) {
  patient_text <- glue::glue(
    "{patient_text}
    This includes {single_patient_mps}."
  )
}

coherence_text <- glue::glue(
  "For this value of k, {length(low_coherence_mps)} metaprogram(s) do not pass the minimum coherence of 0.1. "
)

if (length(low_coherence_mps) > 0) {
  coherence_text <- glue::glue(
    "{coherence_text}
    This includes {low_coherence_mps}."
  )
}
knitr::asis_output(
  glue::glue(
    "
    {main_text}
    
    {patient_text}
    
    {coherence_text}
    "
  )
)
```

```{r}
# finally export the value of k to a file to use for scoring in the next process
# want to export a number to match n_metaprograms in nextflow
optimal_k <- stringr::str_remove(optimal_k, "k_") |> as.numeric()
readr::write_lines(optimal_k, params$output_k_file)
```
